analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes for high earners and corporations, cuts Medicaid and SNAP, and expands oil, gas, and coal leasing.
analysis.headline: Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on near party-line votes of 215-214 in the House and 51-50 in the Senate, and the President signed it into law on July 4, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This reconciliation bill makes the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent — including the 37% top rate — raises the estate tax exemption to $15 million, and adds new deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest, and seniors through 2028. It pays for part of that by tightening Medicaid and SNAP: 80-hour monthly work requirements, twice-yearly eligibility checks, new state cost-sharing, and cuts to noncitizen eligibility. It also lowers federal oil, gas, and coal royalties, mandates new lease sales, and repeals most clean-energy tax credits and environmental grant programs, while adding roughly $150 billion for defense and tens of billions for immigration enforcement, and raising the debt limit by $5 trillion.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners gain permanently through the extended 37% rate, a $40,000 SALT cap, and a $15 million estate and gift tax exemption. Corporations get permanent full expensing, expanded international tax deductions, and lower minimum taxes. Oil, gas, and coal companies get more leasing on federal land, lower royalties, no royalty on vented methane, and drilling-cost deductions under the corporate minimum tax. Defense contractors, shipbuilders, and missile makers get about $150 billion. For-profit colleges regain ground as new borrower-protection rules are delayed until 2035. Working people get temporary help — deductions for tips and overtime and a $2,200 child tax credit — plus reauthorized farm subsidy programs, expanded crop insurance, a $10 billion-a-year rural health fund, and a revived radiation-exposure compensation program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and industry

how_it_helps.text: Establishes deductions of up to $25,000 for tip income and $12,500 for overtime through 2028, phasing out above $150,000 ($300,000 joint) in income.
Raises the child tax credit to $2,200 per child and adds a temporary $6,000 extra deduction for taxpayers 65 and older through 2028.
Creates a $10 billion-per-year rural health program for 2026-2030 and requires Medicaid to pay for out-of-state providers treating children.
Bans spread pricing and requires pass-through pricing from pharmacy benefit managers in Medicaid, and limits PBMs in Medicare to flat service fees starting in 2028.
Reestablishes and expands the Radiation Exposure Compensation program for people harmed by nuclear testing and uranium mining, adding Idaho, New Mexico, and Manhattan Project downwind communities.

Extends farm subsidy programs (Price Loss Coverage, Agriculture Risk Coverage, Dairy Margin Coverage) through crop year 2031, raises reference prices, adds up to 30 million base acres, and raises the ARC/PLC payment cap to $155,000.

analysis.who_pays: Low-income adults lose the most: Medicaid expansion enrollees face 80-hour monthly work requirements, twice-yearly redeterminations, and up to $35 per-visit cost sharing starting in 2026-2029, and states must pick up 5-15% of SNAP benefit costs and 75% of SNAP administrative costs. Noncitizens, including refugees, asylum seekers, and DACA recipients, lose Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP, and premium-tax-credit eligibility. States lose federal matching for provider taxes and higher hospital payment rates. Clean-energy buyers and builders lose vehicle, home, and grid tax credits; EV owners pay a new $250 federal registration fee ($100 for hybrids). Future taxpayers carry the bill from a $5 trillion debt-limit increase, and low-income communities lose dozens of rescinded environmental and air-quality grant programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicaid and SNAP recipients, states, future taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The tip, overtime, senior, and car-loan-interest deductions all expire after 2028, while the high-earner and corporate provisions — the 37% rate, $15 million estate exemption, full expensing, and international tax cuts — are permanent.
The bill raises the debt limit by $5 trillion while cutting taxes and adding new defense, border, and detention spending.

SNAP work requirements now reach adults up to 65, parents of children 14 and older, and veterans and homeless individuals, and states must contribute up to 15% of benefit costs based on payment error rates.

Medicaid expansion adults face monthly 80-hour work or community-engagement requirements and new cost sharing of up to $35 per service beginning no later than the first quarter of 2027, with enforcement beginning in 2026.
Rules that let defrauded student borrowers discharge loans (borrower defense and closed-school discharges) are delayed until July 2035, restoring stricter 2020-era standards in the meantime.

The CAFE fuel-economy civil penalty is set to $0, removing NHTSA's main enforcement tool, and federal royalty rates for oil, gas, and coal are lowered, including ending royalties on methane lost to venting or flaring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine gains for working people — the tip, overtime, and senior deductions and the higher child tax credit — are real but temporary, expiring after 2028, while the bill's largest and permanent benefits go to high earners, large estates, and corporations. The budget is balanced on the other side by the deepest changes to Medicaid and SNAP in decades, a $5 trillion debt-limit increase, and the elimination of most clean-energy credits and environmental programs. Its defenders would point to the rural hospital fund, PBM curbs, farm supports, and border and defense spending as wins; its critics would note the working-class tax relief is a small share of the total and sunsets while the concentrated-interest provisions do not.

outcome.mechanism: A reconciliation bill reported by the House Budget Committee passed the House by one vote, cleared the Senate 51-50 with the Vice President breaking the tie after Republicans defeated roughly twenty amendment and commit motions, and was signed by the President on July 4, 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was a reconciliation package submitted by 11 House committees under the FY2025 budget resolution; reconciliation bills move on expedited Senate procedures that block a filibuster and limit amendments.
The House Budget Committee reported the original measure on May 20, 2025, under a closed rule, and the House passed it 215-214 with one member voting present on May 22.
The Senate defeated more than a dozen motions to commit the bill to committees with instructions between June 30 and July 1, 2025, with all votes splitting on party lines.
The Senate passed the bill 51-50 on July 1, 2025, with the Vice President casting the deciding vote; three Republicans and every Democrat and Independent voted no.
The House agreed to the Senate amendment 218-214 on July 3, 2025, and the President signed it into law as Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025.

The final law increases the debt limit by $5 trillion, makes the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent, raises the estate exemption to $15 million, imposes Medicaid work requirements and cost sharing, expands SNAP work requirements and state cost-sharing, and lowers federal oil, gas, and coal royalties while mandating new lease sales.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners, large estates, and corporations gained permanent tax cuts; oil, gas, coal, and defense companies gained leasing, royalties, and contract dollars; for-profit colleges saw borrower-protection rules delayed. Because the bill passed, Medicaid and SNAP recipients are the side that lost ground.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, estates, and energy, defense, and finance interests

for.name: Jodey Arrington
for.role: Chair, House Budget Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, reported it from the Budget Committee as an original measure, and moved the House to agree to the Senate amendment.

for.name: Senate Republican majority
for.role: 53 Senate Republicans advancing the reconciliation bill
for.what_they_did: Moved the bill to the floor, defeated every Democratic motion to commit it to committee, waived a budget-act point of order, and passed it 51-50.

for.name: JD Vance
for.role: Vice President of the United States
for.what_they_did: Cast the tie-breaking vote on final Senate passage of the bill.

for.name: President Trump
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on July 4, 2025, making it Public Law 119-21.

against.name: House and Senate Democrats
against.role: Minority in both chambers (212 House votes; 45 Democrats plus 2 Independents in the Senate)
against.what_they_did: Voted unanimously against passage in both chambers and offered roughly twenty motions to commit the bill to committees with instructions to change it.

against.name: Three Senate Republicans
against.role: Republican senators who crossed party lines on final passage
against.what_they_did: Joined all Democrats and Independents in voting against final Senate passage, 51-50, nearly defeating the bill.

against.name: Rep. Lori Trahan
against.what_they_did: Offered the motion to recommit the bill to the Budget Committee, which failed 212-216, the last procedural chance to amend it before the vote.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: the House passed it 215-214 with 215 Republicans for and 2 against, no Democrat for; the Senate passed it 51-50 with 50 Republicans for, 3 against, and the Vice President breaking the tie, while all 45 Democrats and 2 Independents voted no.

industries.note: The permanent extension of the 37% top rate, a $40,000 SALT cap, and a $15 million estate tax exemption deliver the largest and most durable tax cuts in the bill, funded partly by reductions in Medicaid and SNAP and by added federal borrowing.

The bill mandates new onshore, offshore, ANWR, and NPR-A lease sales, lowers minimum royalties, reinstates noncompetitive leasing, ends royalties on methane lost to venting or flaring, allows drilling-cost deductions under the corporate minimum tax, and cuts the CAFE penalty to $0. The revenue the government forgoes comes at a direct cost to taxpayers and the Treasury.

industries.industry: Defense contractors, shipbuilders, and missile manufacturers
industries.note: The bill adds roughly $150 billion for shipbuilding ($29.2 billion), missile defense ($24.4 billion), munitions ($25.4 billion), nuclear forces ($14.7 billion), drones, and aircraft. Service members gain housing, pay, and child-care funding; the cost is federal debt.

industries.industry: Clean energy and electric vehicle industries
industries.note: The bill terminates the $7,500 clean vehicle credit, residential and commercial clean energy credits, clean hydrogen, and manufacturing credits, and accelerates phaseouts of wind and solar credits. Consumers and the industry lose the incentives together, raising effective prices for EVs, heat pumps, and solar.

Medicaid coverage reductions, twice-yearly redeterminations, limits on state-directed hospital payments to Medicare rates, and provider-tax restrictions cut hospital revenue; a $10 billion-a-year rural health transformation program partially offsets losses in rural areas. When hospitals lose paying volume, cost shifting and closures follow for patients.

Rules that allow defrauded borrowers to discharge loans (borrower defense to repayment and closed-school discharges) are delayed until July 2035 and replaced with stricter 2020-era standards, and new loan limits replace some accountability mechanisms. Students defrauded by closed or misleading programs bear the cost.

The bill bans spread pricing in Medicaid and limits Medicare PBM compensation to flat service fees with price reporting. Their loss corresponds to lower drug costs for programs that serve ordinary patients.

The bill raises crop subsidy reference prices, expands base acres by up to 30 million, raises the payment cap to $155,000 per person, and waives the income limit (formerly $900,000 AGI) for operations deriving 75% of income from farming. Larger operators capture the gains; the cost is federal spending.
